cf.title: Enlarge the syslogger pipe on Linux (F_SETPIPE_SZ)

input.subject: Enlarge the syslogger pipe on Linux (F_SETPIPE_SZ)

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived the panel, so nothing stops the proposal at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated, message #1 gives measurements for statement logging and bursts, and the change adds no user-visible surface and falls back to the kernel default. Confidence is low because only one message exists, nobody has replied, and the code was not read.

brief.title: Enlarge the syslogger pipe to 1 MiB on Linux with F_SETPIPE_SZ
brief.problem: Backends block in write() when the 64 KiB syslogger pipe fills, and it fills fast when several backends log multi-chunk messages at once. The author targets chatty logging: statement logging, pgaudit, auto_explain and similar.
brief.proposed_design: At pipe creation the syslogger asks the kernel for 1 MiB with F_SETPIPE_SZ, then retries smaller sizes if the kernel refuses. It never shrinks the pipe below what the kernel already gave it. If the fcntl is missing or every request fails, the default stays.
author_claims: At 96 clients with log_min_duration_statement = 0, p99 latency drops from about 10.7 ms to 2.0 ms, but p50 rises from 387 to 509 us.
Collector CPU drops by about a third because it wakes less often and reads more per wakeup.
In RAISE LOG burst tests the patch won every pair on average latency, up to about 8 times lower.
Throughput stays within 1% when the collector is saturated, and 256 KiB gave only a third of the burst gain.
No GUC is needed because 1 MiB is the default unprivileged maximum and the buffer exists once per cluster.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. Nobody has replied.
unclear: The proposal does not say which smaller sizes the retry tries, or whether it logs a failed request.
The author does not discuss the higher p50 latency at 64 and 96 clients as a regression or a trade-off.
The proposal does not say whether pipe-max-size or per-user pipe memory limits can make the request fail on common distributions.
Windows is left out, and the thread does not say whether a CreatePipe size change would follow.
The thread does not say how a larger buffer changes log loss or ordering if the syslogger dies or restarts.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a Linux-only F_SETPIPE_SZ path with a retry loop in syslogger.c, and leaves Windows unchanged.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The pipe size changes how long logging backends block in write(); p50 rises from 387 to 509 us at 96 clients.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Is the higher p50 at 64 and 96 clients (387 to 509 us at 96) an accepted trade-off, and does it appear when the box is not oversubscribed?
Which smaller sizes does the retry try, and does the syslogger report the size it got or a failed request?
Can pipe-max-size or the per-user pipe-user-pages-soft limit make the 1 MiB request fail, or shrink other pipes of the postgres user, on common distributions?
Do the results hold with logs on a real disk instead of tmpfs, where the collector's write speed differs?
Does a 1 MiB buffer change how much log data is lost or reordered when the syslogger dies or restarts?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the syslogger and postmaster startup code, and Linux pipe semantics, would have to own it. Nobody has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a Linux-only fcntl path in syslogger.c and for a latency shift under heavy logging: lower p99, higher p50 when oversubscribed. The path is small and falls back to the kernel default, so the long-term burden is low.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way. The author says he cannot test the Windows CreatePipe variant.

priority.reason: The patch is 2.5 KiB in one file with no GUC or other user-visible surface, and message #1 shows gains for statement logging, pgaudit and auto_explain workloads. The open points are the p50 trade-off and kernel limit behaviour, which a reviewer can settle quickly.

provisional_note: Without the code, the retry sizes, the handling of a failed or partly granted request, and any reporting of the final pipe size could not be checked. The effect of kernel per-user pipe limits also rests on the code and on testing.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve logrotate test so that it meaningfully exercises syslogger.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Improve logrotate test so that it meaningfully exercises syslogger.
Reverted commit(s): Don't do pg_ctl logrotate test on Windows
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Discussion of bug #15804 reveals that this test didn't really prove
that the syslogger child process ever launched successfully, much
less did anything.  It was only checking that the expected log file
gets created, and that's done in the postmaster.  Moreover, the
test assumed it could rename the log file, which is likely to fail
on Windows (cf. commit d611175e5).

Instead, use the default log file name pattern, which should result
in a new file name being chosen after 1 second, and verify that
rotation has occurred by checking for a new file name.  Also add code
to test that messages actually do propagate through the syslogger.

In theory this version of the test should work on Windows, so
revert d611175e5.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pipelining/batch mode support for libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a batch mode to libpq, so a client can send many queries without waiting for each result and read the results later in order. New functions enter and leave batch mode, mark the end of a batch with a Sync message, and step through the queue of pending results.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund moved it out of v10 because the libpq API could not be changed later and needed more review. The test module also kept failing its COPY case. In later rounds he found many small send() calls that needed coalescing without unbounded buffering, plus naming, documentation and memory-use problems. The author promised a new version but did not post it before the commitfest closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Based on the discussions in this thread, and that a new version hasn’t been
submitted, I’m marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pipelining/batch mode support for libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a batch (pipelining) mode to libpq, so a client can send many queries asynchronously without waiting for each result and then read the results in order. It adds new functions to enter and leave batch mode, mark batch ends with a Sync, and process the result queue, plus docs and a C test module.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was returned because review feedback stayed unaddressed: after the March 2018 review by Kyotaro HORIGUCHI no new version came, and by October 2018 the patch no longer applied. Earlier, Andres Freund refused to rush it into v10 because the libpq API could not be changed later, and asked for API renames, fewer libpq round trips through coalesced sends, and bounded memory use. Open problems also included COPY inside a batch, which left the connection out of sync.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Unfortunately, nothing was changed since then, so there is already some amount of unaddressed review feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Shared-memory based stats collector
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the file-based stats collector with statistics kept in dynamic shared memory (dshash), so backends read stats without a stats file written by a separate process. The stats collector process goes away, and per-kind stats code moves into new files under utils/activity.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reworked the patch in spring 2021 and judged it not committable for v14, citing weak test coverage, the need for architectural review and performance testing, an unresolved case where stats for dropped functions can be revived, and many open FIXMEs. A rebase then stalled on a new issue with partitioned tables. No new version was posted after July 2021, so the CommitFest manager marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately I think
that, while it has gotten a lot closer, it's still about a week's worth of
work away from being committable.

precedents_retrieved.title: logicalctl: release LogicalDecodingControlLock before logging
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moved the ereport(LOG) in DisableLogicalDecoding() so that it runs after LogicalDecodingControlLock is released. The goal was to keep code that could do unexpected work, such as an errcontext callback doing catalog lookups, out of an LWLock section where a deadlock would go undetected.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada found the change unnecessary because only the startup and checkpointer processes disable logical decoding, and they do not access system catalogs, so an errcontext callback carries little or no deadlock risk. He also noted that logging after the release could put the "disabled" message after a concurrent "enabled" message. Michael Paquier said LWLocks have no rule against elog() while held and the code path does not matter for performance. The author then withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Given that these processes don't access system catalogs for example, I think there is little or zero risk of a deadlock occurring even if we do something in errcontext.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't ignore recovery conflict interrupt on blocked writing
precedents_retrieved.summary: On a standby, a backend blocked writing results to a stuck or dead client ignores interrupts, so its buffer pin can block WAL replay until the TCP retransmission timeout, which can be about 15 minutes. The patch makes ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() handle recovery conflict interrupts during a blocked write and terminate the session, with a new Perl module for raw protocol tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund found that the patch did not promote the ERROR to FATAL, so the session was not really terminated. He also showed that the backend often reaches ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() with interrupts held, for example while sending an error message, and then the conflict is never resolved. The author posted a reworked approach on 2025-01-21. No reply follows in the visible messages, and they do not say why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Unfortunately I suspect that this means any protection we'd get from this version of the patch is rather incomplete - if the recovery conflict is triggered while not blocked, we'll ERROR out and report the message with interrupts held.

precedents_retrieved.title: Adding linux cachestat in file Readv and Prefetch
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses the Linux 6.5 cachestat() syscall in file reads and prefetch to collect page cache statistics for a file range. It also stops prefetching when recently evicted pages suggest memory pressure.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra doubted that per-file cachestat data from one 1GB segment detects memory pressure, and he disagreed that prefetching should stop under memory pressure. He also noted that the patch had no performance evaluation. Robert Haas agreed and said pg_prewarm should read what the user asks for, and the thread does not show why the feature is needed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm not sure I even agree with the idea that we should stop prefetching
when there is memory pressure. IMHO it's perfectly fine to keep
prefetching stuff even if it triggers eviction of unnecessary pages from
page cache.

precedents_retrieved.title: Deletion of the recycled future WAL files to free-up disk space if max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off
precedents_retrieved.summary: When max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off, a checkpoint should delete recycled future WAL files to free disk space. The author suggested keeping recycled WAL files in a sorted list and, at checkpoint, deleting them from the newest end, rebuilding the list after restart if needed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No patch was ever posted, so the commitfest entry had nothing to review. Jacob Champion closed it for that reason and invited the author to reopen it if a patch existed. Justin Pryzby supported the idea, and Tom Lane questioned only whether the behaviour was real.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:

of this thread, so I don't think there's anything to review.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix buffer pinning logic/visibility bugs in [SP-]Gist Index-Only Scans
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Geoghegan (pgeoghegan), Michail Nikolaev (nkey), Matthias van de Meent (mmeent), Mihail Nikalayeu (mihailnikalayeu)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a race in GiST and SP-GiST index-only scans, where concurrent VACUUM can remove a TID and set the visibility map bit before the scan checks it, so a dead tuple is returned. Later versions drop the idea of holding pins on index pages: they add a table AM API (table_index_vischeck_tuples) so the index AM checks the visibility map while it still holds the page pin, and they also change nbtree to use it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible message (v14, December 2025) only fixes a CFBot failure, and the entry was withdrawn about six months later with no visible objection or explanation. The author had moved a backpatchable version of the fix to a separate thread.

roaster_notes.note: The precedent list has no earlier proposal to enlarge the syslogger pipe or use F_SETPIPE_SZ, and the thread does not point to one. From the prior-attempts angle there is no recorded rejection reason to apply, so no precedent found.

From the standards and compatibility angle the patch has no user-facing contract to judge: no syntax, no GUC, no catalog entry, no pg_dump state and no psql change, and it falls back to the kernel default when the fcntl fails. The higher p50 latency at 64 and 96 clients and the unstated retry sizes belong to the performance and design angles.

The patch changes only the kernel buffer size of the syslogger pipe in syslogger.c, with no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or ABI change. The postmaster holds both pipe ends across syslogger restarts, so buffered log data survives a collector restart as before, and nothing persistent needs pg_upgrade or replication handling.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. The pipe stays internal to the cluster, owned by the postgres OS user, and no new SQL surface, setting or role is added. A database user who floods the log with RAISE LOG could already block backends, and a larger buffer reduces that blocking instead of adding a new denial-of-service path. The extra kernel memory is one fixed 1 MiB buffer. Without the code I could not check one thing: whether the request counts against the postgres user's pipe-user-pages-soft limit in a way that shrinks other pipes, such as archive_command. That is an operations question, not a security one.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is no objection worth sending. The patch is a best-effort fcntl in one file with no GUC, catalog, protocol or API surface, and it falls back to current behaviour. Its costs (one kernel buffer per cluster, a higher p50 under oversubscription) fall on clusters that log heavily, which are the clusters that gain. Two points cannot be checked without the code: which retry sizes the patch tries, and whether it reports the size it got.

Postgres has no existing setting, view or idiom that sets the syslogger pipe size. On Linux the size can only be changed with fcntl on the open pipe, and pipe-max-size caps requests without changing the default, so an administrator cannot get this from outside. The pipe is created in the postmaster before extensions could act on it. Switching log_destination to syslog avoids the pipe but changes delivery and loss behaviour, so it does not do the same job.

No demand objection. Statement logging, pgaudit and auto_explain are common workloads, message #1 shows measured gains for them, and the cost (one 1 MiB kernel buffer, no GUC, no UI) falls only on clusters that log heavily. The p50 trade-off at 64 and 96 clients and the missing retry details belong to the design and performance angles.
